title: The American Ship That Vanished Without a Trace
sources: Wikipedia, 'USS Cyclops': 306 crew and passengers lost without a trace sometime after March 4, 1918; unscheduled stop in Barbados, water over the Plimsoll line (overloaded); no wreckage ever found
Tara Ross (TDIH) / SNAC: 10,800 long tons (about 11,000 tons) of manganese ore, much denser than coal; Wilson: 'Only God and the sea know what happened to the great ship'
SNAC / Daily Kos (US Navy photo): left Barbados March 4, 1918 with her starboard engine inoperative due to a cracked cylinder, bound for Baltimore
History UK / Naval History magazine (USNI): largest loss of life outside of combat in US Navy history
NHHC H-Gram 016: sister ships Proteus and Nereus vanished in 1941 with cargoes of bauxite ore
Wikipedia: declared lost by the Navy on June 1, 1918

lines.text: In March 1918, a giant US Navy ship sailed out of Barbados,
lines.caps: In March | 1918,~nineteen | a giant | US Navy | ship | sailed | out of | Barbados,

lines.text: with three hundred and six people on board,
and then it simply vanished.
No distress call, no wreckage, no bodies,
nothing, ever.
She was the USS Cyclops,
a coal ship carrying almost eleven thousand tons of heavy ore,
lines.caps: a coal | ship | carrying | almost | 11,000 tons~eleven | of heavy | ore,

lines.text: so heavy she sat below her safety line.
And one of her two engines was broken,
so she limped north toward Baltimore on just one.
The Navy searched and searched,
but found nothing.
Even President Wilson said only God and the sea know what happened to her.
But here's the creepy part:
in 1941, two of her sister ships,
lines.caps: in 1941,~nineteen | two | of her | sister | ships,

lines.text: also carrying heavy ore,
vanished too, without a trace.
It's still the Navy's biggest loss of life outside of combat,
and more than a hundred years later,
no one has ever found her.
So... where did the Cyclops go?
